titre: Six Islets Emptied of Life to Test a Theory
accroche: In 1966, two biologists cover six mangrove islets with a tarp and gas them, to time the return of life.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the Florida Keys, tiny islets of red mangrove, eleven to eighteen meters across, have no dry land at all: only the branches and aerial roots shelter life, almost exclusively climbing arthropods, spiders, ants, weevils, psocids. In 1966, the ecologist Daniel Simberloff, then a doctoral student, and his advisor E.O. Wilson first take an exhaustive census of the fauna of six of these islets, then cover them with a tarp and gas them with methyl bromide, a fumigant that kills arthropods without harming the mangroves. The aim is not to destroy: it is to start from a known inventory to observe, in real time, how an animal community rebuilds itself.

## The Theory They Wanted to Put to the Test

The experiment tests a model published three years earlier by Robert MacArthur and E.O. Wilson, which they would develop in a 1967 book: the theory of island biogeography. It proposes that the number of species living on an island at a given moment results from a balance between two opposing flows, the arrival of new species, faster near a source of colonizers, and their local disappearance, faster on a small island, where populations stay tiny and die out easily. The number of species stabilizes, but which ones occupy the island changes constantly.

It is a precise prediction, and therefore testable. Simberloff and Wilson monitor the six gassed islets for two years. In a little under a year, the number of arthropod species returns close to its level before the fumigation, faster on the islets near the source mangrove than on the more isolated ones, as the model predicts. But two years after the methyl bromide, on almost all the islets, fewer than 40% of the species present are those that lived there before the experiment. The number comes back; the identity does not.

## From an Island Theory to a Rule for Nature Reserves

The theory does not stop at islands surrounded by water. A forest ringed by fields, a reserve ringed by roads, work by the same logic: a habitat isolated in the midst of a hostile environment. In 1975, the biologist Jared Diamond drew from it a practical rule for conservation: for equal total area, one large reserve protects more species than several small ones. The recommendation spread quickly in the management of parks and reserves.

Simberloff, the author of the gassed-islet experiment, himself challenged this extrapolation the following year, with the zoologist Lawrence Abele: the rule assumes that the species of small reserves form a subset of those of large ones. If each small reserve shelters species absent from the others, several small reserves can add up to more species than a single large one. The debate that followed, known as SLOSS, for single large or several small, occupied conservation ecology for two decades. It is still not settled in absolute terms: the answer depends on how the habitat was lost, on the size of the home ranges of the species concerned, and on the connectivity between the remaining fragments. A theory born of carefully gassed and then counted islets was not enough, on its own, to say how to design a reserve.

repere.texte: A little under a year after the fumigation, the number of arthropod species on the islets recovers its initial level; but two years later, on almost all the islets, fewer than 40% of the species present are those that lived there before the experiment.
repere.source: Simberloff, D. & Wilson, E.O., “Experimental Zoogeography of Islands: A Two-Year Record of Colonization,” Ecology, 51(6), 1970

carte.punch: Two biologists gassed six small islets to observe, in real time, how life rebuilds itself there.
carte.idee: In 1966, Daniel Simberloff and E.O. Wilson eliminate all the fauna of six mangrove islets to test the theory of island biogeography. The number of species comes back within a year, but they are not the same ones. The theory later inspired conservation rules, still debated.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: In English; traces the debate between Diamond and Simberloff and its current state.

quiz.question: What does the Simberloff and Wilson gassed-islet experiment show, once the number of species has returned to normal?
choix: That life never fully returns after a local extinction
That exactly the same species recolonize each islet
That the number of species returns to its initial level, but their identity has largely changed
That only the largest islets regain their original diversity
quiz.explication: The number of species recovered in under a year, in line with MacArthur and Wilson's equilibrium model. But two years after the fumigation, fewer than 40% of the species present on most islets were those from before: the theory predicts a stable number of species, not a fixed composition. Islet size, in this experiment, was not correlated with the number of species.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where did the experiment take place, and what was distinctive about these islets?
choix: On a large volcanic island in the Pacific, entirely covered in dense tropical forest
In an Arctic archipelago, on rocky islets entirely devoid of vegetation
Along an Amazonian river, on temporary, unstable sandbars
In the Florida Keys, on mangrove islets with no dry land, populated by climbing arthropods
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The experiment takes place in the Florida Keys, on tiny islets of red mangrove with no dry land, where only the branches and aerial roots shelter a fauna of climbing arthropods.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which theory does the experiment test, and when was it published relative to the experiment?
choix: MacArthur and Wilson's theory of island biogeography, published three years before the experiment
Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection, published a century earlier
A theory proposed by Simberloff himself, the year before the experiment
Clements's theory of ecological climaxes, published the same year as the experiment
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The experiment tests the model published by MacArthur and Wilson in 1963, three years before the 1966 experiment, and developed into a book in 1967, only after it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Simberloff himself argue, in 1976, against the conservation rule proposed by Diamond?
choix: That the size of a nature reserve never has any effect on the number of species it shelters
That several small reserves can bring together more species than a single large reserve of the same total size
That only very large reserves can effectively protect the most threatened species
That the rule proposed by Diamond applies only to true islands, never to land reserves
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Simberloff himself, with Lawrence Abele, challenges Diamond's extrapolation: if each small reserve shelters species absent from the others, several small reserves can add up to more species than a single large one.
